comment.value:
This paper introduces a new benchmark dataset, WikiDo, a dataset to evaluate the out-of-domain (OOD) generalizability of vision-language cross-modal retrieval models. The dataset contains newly collected image-text pairs drawn from Wikipedia Diversity Observatory, including 354K training samples, human-verified in-distribution (ID) test set (3K) and OOD test set (3K). The experimental results with CLIP and BLIP show that even if a model shows a superior performance on popular benchmarks (e.g., MS-COCO), it can show an inferior performance on the proposed OOD benchmark. It is observed not only in terms of zero-shot classification but also in fine-tuning; even fine-tuning to the proposed training samples only improves OOD scores moderately.

This paper has three expert reviews, mostly on the positive side. The raised concerns by the reviewers were mostly addressed by the authors' responses. For example, they addressed the concerns regarding the OOD test sample extension (GkTz, sRnE), writing quality (GkTz, sRnE) or pre-training data leakage (UUyd). I personally think that the concern regarding the model diversity (e.g., only CLIP and BLIP variants are considered) raised by the reviewer UUyd is not well addressed, but it can be minor considering the purpose of this paper. Also, as the reviewer sRnE pointed out, this paper should open their script and leaderboard. Assuming that the authors are ready to open their leaderboard to Kaggle (as they clarified in their rebuttal), I think this concern can be addressed.

Overall, after the author-reviewer discussion, all the reviewers agreed that this paper exceeds the acceptance threshold of the NeurIPS D&B track. I agree with the reviewers and recommend acceptance.
Thank you for your response. I will keep my initial rating.

rebuttal.value:
Thank you for the careful review and feedback. Please find our responses inline:

>**1. Limited number of topics in the dataset**

- The list of topics and labels for the articles are adopted from Wikipedia Diversity Observatory. The Wikipedia Diversity Observatory has an effective pipeline for assigning the topic labels to the Wikipedia articles. Each Wikipedia article is tagged by human editors with certain properties and items. Articles with items related to a topic are classified into that topic. We rely on these topics to characterize the ID-OOD nature of our data splits.

- We note that the selected topics also encompass a number of subtopics that we do not explicitly include as part of our metadata. The range of subtopics shows the generality of the topics. We will include this in a revised version of our dataset. A sample pie plot of top subtopics can be seen in Figure 1 (in the rebuttal pdf).

- As we mention in Section 3.1 in our submission, this dataset is only one part of the original source (Wikipedia Diversity Observatory). There are other axes of diversity that can be used to test different axes of generalizations. These include: geographical location, cultural context, gender, sexual orientation, ethnic groups and religious groups. We aim to explore this direction as future work.


>**2. WikiDO has only one ID-OOD split. Moreover, OOD  test set has only three topics**

- That's a great point! Previous benchmarks [1,2] on domain generalization have shown that the performance (z-shot and fine tuning) of VLMs is considerably high for both ID and OOD test splits. This is due to high similarity between the elements of these test splits as shown in [3] and Table 10 in the submission. Our goal is to create a hard OOD test split which shares the same source (Wikipedia image-text pairs) as the training data and ID-test split BUT still is very dissimilar w.r.t. to the topics. Therefore, in order to obtain our hard OOD test split, we compute the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between all topics and find only three topics to be very dissimilar from the rest of the topics, as mentioned in Section 3.2 (Table 9). The tSNE plots (Figure 3) also show higher dissimilarity with the rest of the topics, thus making the OOD split limited to three topics only. As future work, we could certainly create multiple ID-OOD test splits with our curated data and measure the ID-OOD gaps, but in this work our goal was to show one “hard” ID-OOD setup where the domains are vastly different.

>**3. Figure 3 is not a proper way to visualize overlapping regions. It needs to be improved.**

- Thank you for the suggestion to improve Figure 3. Based on your inputs, we have a new version as shown in the rebuttal pdf which we will update in the revised version.



**References**:
>
>[1] Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge J. Belongie, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, Piotr Dollár, and C. Lawrence Zitnick. Microsoft coco: Common objects in context. In European Conference on Computer Vision, 2014.
>
>[2] Peter Young, Alice Lai, Micah Hodosh, and J. Hockenmaier. From image descriptions to visual denotations: New similarity metrics for semantic inference over event descriptions. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2:67–78, 2014.
>
>[3] Yuchen Ren, Zhendong Mao, Shancheng Fang, Yan Lu, Tong He, Hao Du, Yongdong Zhang, and Wanli Ouyang. Crossing the gap: Domain generalization for image captioning. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, pages 2871–2880, 393 2023.

rebuttal.value:
Thank you for the informative review and suggestions. Please find our responses below.

>**1. The distribution discrepancy lies in the training and testing data. How do we know whether the data in the downstream task has been seen in the pre-training stage?**

That's a valid question! Our dataset is derived from Wikipedia, therefore there is a high chance that these images  are already part of the big pretraining mixtures in VLMs. However, the captions extracted from Wikipedia are noisy. So, it is possible that they may have been filtered during the pretraining stage of these VLMs. Moreover, we use an enhanced version of these captions, which are unlikely to be present exactly in the pretraining data.
 
>**2. In the experimental results, the authors only consider the BILP and CLIP models. Results of more vision-language models should be reported.**

Thank you for the suggestion! For the task of image-text retrieval, MSCOCO and Flickr-3k test sets are the most popularly used benchmarks. We selected models currently performing best on these benchmarks i.e. BLIP, BLIP2 and CLIP of varying sizes. Therefore, we selected the same high-performant models on our benchmark as well for a fair comparison. Moreover, we compare the performance across multiple model sizes (~200M, ~500M, 1.1B parameters), fine-tuning methods varying the number of data samples. As future work, we do plan to extend to newer tasks and evaluate more VLMs.

>**3. The experiments should conduct multiple runs and Mean $\pm$ std performance should be reported.**

The experiments are compute-expensive as the fine tuning set contains a minimum of 100K image-text pairs. We do train CLIP (the best-performing model on WIKIDO) using two different random seeds. As shown in Table 4 in the supplementary material, the variance across the two runs is marginal.

Thank you for the positive review and feedback. Please find our response inline: 
>**1. There are few typos e.g., @L261 "can be bri by adding"**

Thank you for pointing out the typos. We will fix them in the revised version. 

>**2. Authors should add scripts to automatically update leaderboard. Also, add the code to replicate their baseline results (this is not available now)**

That's an excellent suggestion! We are working on creating automated scripts to update the leaderboard. In fact, we are considering hosting the leaderboard on Kaggle for more visibility and ease of use. We used existing codebases to implement the baselines without any changes. The link to the central repository to replicate the baselines will be updated on the website. 

>**3. Is it hard to extend test set?**

The test set can be extended!  As suggested in Section 3.1, other axes of diversity (like geographical location, cultural context, gender, sexual orientation, ethnic groups and religious groups) can be used to further create complex datasets and benchmarks to test the generalizations of VLMs on multiple axes. Additionally, interested researchers could create different combinations of ID-OOD test splits.

title.value: Meaningful improvement in cross-modal retrieval benchmark

summary_and_contributions.value: The paper introduces WikiDO, a new benchmark dataset designed to evaluate both in-domain (ID) and out-of-domain (OOD) performance in cross-modal retrieval tasks. WikiDO is based on image-text pairs from Wikipedia. The authors argue that current OOD benchmarks using MSCOCO and Flickr with cross-finetuning are inadequate, and WikiDO serves as a suitable alternative. Experimental results highlight the limitations of the MSCOCO and Flickr cross-finetuning settings and demonstrate WikiDO's effectiveness as an OOD benchmark for cross-modal retrieval.

review.value:
The paper clearly describes the need for a new benchmark on OOD cross-modal retrieval and supports this claim with proper empirical results. The writing quality is good enough to understand WikiDO's motivation and contributions. I believe WikiDO can make a significant contribution to future research on cross-modal retrieval as a new decent benchmark for OOD performance.

Pros
- Well-motivated dataset and good writing quality
- Tables 4 and 5 clearly show the problem of the existing benchmark, which is solved by WikiDO.
- As shown in Tables 3 and 4, performance ranking is different from the previous benchmark. Thus, WikiDO can provide a new perspective on cross-modal retrieval benchmarks. 

Cons
- The dataset has limited topics, and the OOD test set only has three topics. Thus, it is not enough to evaluate OOD performance on general topics.
- The dataset splits for ID and OOD are fixed. There are no reports of OOD performance on other combinations.
- Figure 3 is not a proper way to visualize overlapping regions. It needs to be improved.

strengths.value:
- Well-motivated dataset and good writing quality
- Tables 4 and 5 clearly show the problem of the existing benchmark, which is solved by WikiDO.
- As shown in Tables 3 and 4, performance ranking is different from the previous benchmark. Thus, WikiDO can provide a new perspective on cross-modal retrieval benchmarks.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
- WikiDO has only one topic split for ID and OOD. Since the number of topics is limited, I doubt it is enough to represent OOD performance for general topics. It would be better if the paper covers OOD performances on different ID / OOD splits.

- Figure 3 looks like orange dots are drawn above blue dots. Thus, it is not possible to find exact overlapping and separated regions. I recommend authors improve the visualization of Figure 3, such as introducing random drawing order, increasing the transparency rate, and reducing the number of dots with random sampling.

limitations.value: Limitations are addressed in the paper.

correctness.value: The claims sound correct and well-supported by experimental results. The dataset is constructed in a valid way. The evaluation looks fair.

relation_to_prior_work.value: The paper points out problem of previous benchmark.

review.value:
This paper proposes a new benchmark dataset to evaluate the OOD generalization capability for Vision-Language Models. The dataset contains 384K image-text pairs from Wikipedia with domain labels, along with in-distribution (ID) and OOD test sets of size 3K each. Experimental results with BLIP and CLIP models are also provided.

Pros:
1) The problem concerned in this paper is important. It is necessary to construct datasets to help better evaluate the OOD generalization ability of vision-language models.
2) The dataset contains 384K image-text pairs, a large-scale dataset.
3) The distribution discrepancy is validated from multiple perspectives.

Cons:
1) The distribution discrepancy lies in the training and testing data. How do we know whether the data in the downstream task has been seen in the pre-training stage?
2) In the experimental results, the authors only consider the BILP and CLIP models. Results of more vision-language models should be reported.
3) The experiments should conduct multiple runs and Mean $\pm$ std performance should be reported.

title.value: WikiDO is a new benchmark for evaluating VLM's cross-modal retrieval

summary_and_contributions.value: Authors propose a new WikiDO benchmark to evaluate generalization to OOD data in VLM's cross-modal retrieval task. Unlike previous benchmarks, WikiDO carefully selects and curates the data including human verification (test set only). Then, authors evaluate popular baseline (CLIP, BLIP-1/2) on the proposed benchmark. Specifically, they consider zero-shot and fine-tuning setups for text to image and image to text retrieval. Experiments show interesting results for the selected baselines.

review.value: Benchmarking of VLMs is an important topic for the research community. In particular, this benchmark is well-motivated, carefully constructed and evaluated recent baselines. Therefore, it can be widely-used to evaluate OOD generalization in VLMs. There are few limitations that are mentioned in the paper (e.g., a relatively small test set with human verification).

strengths.value:
1. Well-written, clearly-motivated and reasonably constructed benchmark. 
2. Web-site, leaderboard and code are available. Probably, authors should add scripts to automatically update leaderboard including the code to replicate their baseline results (this is not available now).
3. Recent baselines have been evaluated.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1. There are few typos e.g., @L261 "can be bri by adding"
2. Authors should add scripts to automatically update leaderboard. Also, add the code to replicate their baseline results (this is not available now)
3. Is it hard to extend test set?

title.value: WikiDO: A New Benchmark Evaluating Cross-Modal Retrieval for Vision-Language Models

TLDR.value: a new dataset and benchmark for evaluating out-of-distribution generalization of vision-language models in cross-modal retrieval

abstract.value: Cross-modal (image-to-text and text-to-image) retrieval is an established task used in evaluation benchmarks to test the performance of vision-language models (VLMs). Several state-of-the-art VLMs (e.g. CLIP, BLIP-2) have achieved near-perfect performance on widely-used image-text retrieval benchmarks such as MSCOCO-Test-5K and Flickr30K-Test-1K. As a measure of out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, prior works rely on zero-shot performance evaluated on one dataset (Flickr) using a VLM finetuned on another one (MSCOCO). We argue that such comparisons are insufficient to assess the OOD generalization capability of models due to high visual and linguistic similarity between the evaluation and finetuning datasets. To address this gap, we introduce WikiDO (drawn from Wikipedia Diversity Observatory), a novel cross-modal retrieval benchmark to assess the OOD generalization capabilities of pretrained VLMs. This consists of newly scraped 380K image-text pairs from Wikipedia with domain labels, a carefully curated, human-verified a)in-distribution (ID) test set (3K) and b) OOD test set (3K). The image-text pairs are very diverse in topics and geographical locations. We evaluate different VLMs of varying capacity on the \wikido benchmark; BLIP-2 achieves zero-shot performance of $R@1\approx66\%$ on the OOD test set, compared to $\approx$ $81\%$ on COCO and $\approx95\%$ on Flickr. When fine-tuned on WikiDO, the $R@1$ improvement is at most $\approx5\%$ on OOD instances compared to $\approx12\%$ on ID instances. We probe the VLMs with varying finetuning objectives and datasets of varying sizes to identify what aids OOD generalization the most. Our results confirm that WikiDO offers a strong cross-modal benchmark for current VLMs in specifically evaluating for OOD generalization. Our benchmark is hosted as a competition at https://kaggle.com/competitions/wikido24 with public access to dataset and code.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
